title: Courrier sud
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
blurb: An airmail pilot flies Toulouse to Dakar: storms over Spain, a night over Morocco, the silence of the Sahara, and a love in Paris he could not carry with him.

p: Here, at Cap Juby, on the coast of the Sahara, we wait for the mail the way you wait for a friend.
The radio has just told us that it left Toulouse this morning, at five forty-five.
In a few hours, it will be flying over Spain; tomorrow, it will land here, on the sand, before setting off again for Dakar.
The pilot is called Jacques Bernis. He is my oldest friend.
I picture him in Toulouse, in the cold of dawn.
The mechanics have warmed up the engine; the bags of letters have been loaded into the plane.

There are love letters in them, contracts, news of births and deaths, which thousands of people have entrusted to the post without knowing that a man alone was going to carry them over the mountains and the sea.
Bernis put on his helmet, he waved, and the plane rolled over the wet grass before rising slowly into the grey sky.
We have known each other since childhood.
Already at ten he was the boldest boy in the class: the one who climbed highest in the trees and was never afraid of being punished.
We grew up in the same little town, we went to the same school, and we shared the same dreams.
In the evening, in the dormitory, we used to talk in low voices about the faraway countries we would discover one day.
It seemed to us that the whole world was waiting for us, and that all we had to do was grow up to possess it.
During the holidays, we often went to visit a childhood friend, Geneviève, in an old house surrounded by a park.
She was fifteen. She knew the name of every tree and every bird, and everything around her seemed solid and eternal.
We both loved her without saying so, the way you love at that age: with a kind of silent admiration.
Later, our paths parted. I left for Africa, and Bernis became an airline pilot.
Geneviève, for her part, married a rich, serious man called Herlin.
From up there, Bernis sees the earth as nobody sees it.
Towns are no more than little grey spots; roads, threads; fields, a carpet of colours.
The people who live down below believe that their houses are solid and that their problems are immense.
Seen from a plane, they seem fragile, and a little touching.
But the pilot does not only look at the landscape. He constantly watches the engine, the compass, the sky.
Above the mountains, near Alicante, the storm was waiting for him.
Rain was beating on the windscreen, the wind was shaking the plane like a leaf, and he could no longer see anything.
He flew for a long time a few metres above the sea, following the coast so as not to get lost.
When he finally landed, his hands were trembling. He laughed, though, like a child who has just escaped a danger.
That is what he loves about this job: every flight is a struggle, and every arrival, a small victory.
Down below, people argue, hesitate, wait. Up there, you have to decide immediately, and the slightest mistake must be paid for.
A few months earlier, Bernis had spent a week's leave in Paris.
He had felt like a stranger in that city where everyone seemed in a hurry, and where nobody ever looked up at the sky.
One evening, almost without meaning to, he went and rang Geneviève's doorbell.
He found her pale and tired. Her son had been ill for several days, and she no longer left his room.
Her husband talked about doctors, bills, and an important dinner that couldn't be cancelled.
Bernis understood at once that she was not happy, and that perhaps she never had been.
Three days later, the child died.
Geneviève did not cry in front of the others. She sat motionless, in the middle of the bouquets of flowers, as if the world had lost its meaning.
On the evening of the funeral, she said to Bernis: 'Take me away. I can't live here any more.'
They left that very night, by car, heading south.
The headlights lit up the wet road, the trees streamed past on either side, and Geneviève, her head against Bernis's shoulder, kept her eyes open without saying anything.
Bernis believed he was taking her towards a new life, truer and freer.
Towards midnight, they stopped at a little country inn.
The room was cold and ugly; the bed creaked; a bare light bulb hung from the ceiling.
Geneviève began to tremble. She looked around her as if she did not understand where she was.
Bernis saw then that she needed her things, her habits, her walls: all that world which he despised and which, for her, was life itself.
At dawn, without their needing to speak, he turned round, and he took her back to Paris.
In front of her door, she squeezed his hand very tightly, the way you say goodbye to someone you will never see again.
A few weeks later, he learned that she had died too, of a fever that nobody had been able to cure.
After Paris, Bernis asked to go back to the line as soon as possible.
Up there, at least, he knew what had to be done.
This evening, he left Casablanca at sunset, and he is now flying towards Agadir, in the night falling over Morocco.
At night, the pilot can no longer see the ground. He sees only the small lights of farms, isolated in the darkness like boats on the sea.
Behind each of these lights, he imagines a family eating dinner, a child doing homework, a woman waiting.
In the past, he would have despised them. Tonight, he envies them a little.
In the cockpit, only the needles of the instruments glow, with a soft green light.
He checks the altitude, the oil pressure, the engine temperature. Everything is fine.
Above him, the stars are so many that he sometimes has trouble telling the sky from the lights on the ground.
He thinks that, if the engine stopped now, nobody in the world could help him. And that thought, strangely, makes him calm.
Towards midnight, he finally catches sight of the lights of the Agadir airfield, lined up in the dark like a sentence written for him.
He throttles back, the plane comes down gently, and the wheels touch the ground.
A mechanic hands him a cup of scalding coffee. Bernis drinks it without saying anything, his eyes still full of stars.
As for me, I have been living at Cap Juby for a year. I am the stopover manager.
Our little post stands at the edge of the sea, next to a Spanish fort, and all around there is nothing but sand, as far as the eye can see.
The Spanish soldiers in the fort are bored. They play cards, write to their families and count the days until the end of their service.
Twice a week, a boat brings fresh water, vegetables and newspapers a fortnight old.
The desert is not empty, though. It is inhabited by tribes who know it better than we do, and some of whom attack lost airmen.
At night, I often go out to look at the stars.
They are so many and so close that you feel you could touch them.
In that immense silence, you understand that life comes down to a few things: water, fire, a friend arriving.
Last night, Bernis landed here, as planned.
We had dinner together under the lamp, talking about our childhood. He only said a few words to me about Geneviève.
'You see,' he said to me, 'I thought I could save her. But you can't carry a woman like a bag of mail.'
He smiled sadly, then he went to bed, because he had to set off again before daylight.
This morning, Bernis's plane took off at five o'clock, and we watched it disappear towards the south.
At eight o'clock, the radio at Port-Étienne should have reported him passing. It reported nothing.
At ten o'clock, still nothing. At midday, we knew that something had happened.
An engine failure, no doubt. Bernis had landed in the middle of the desert before, and he had always come through.
But I was thinking of the tribes, of thirst, of the sun that kills within a few hours those who have no water.
We got a second plane ready, and I set off to look for him with another pilot.
For hours, we flew over the dunes, so low that our plane's shadow ran over the sand beside us.
Everything looked the same: the same waves of sand, the same black rocks, the same sky white with heat.
At last, around four o'clock, I caught sight of a shining shape at the foot of a dune: it was his plane.
One wing was broken, and the propeller was twisted, but the plane had not burned.
Bernis was lying a little further off, on the sand, his arms spread wide, like a man asleep in the sun.
He had been killed while he was repairing his engine. His tools were still beside him.
I stayed on my knees beside him for a long time, unable to think of anything.
Then I looked at the sky, and I thought of everything he had loved: speed, the stars, the freedom of wide open spaces.
Perhaps he had found here what he had been looking for all his life, and what cities had never been able to give him.
The mail bags were intact, in the cabin.
We loaded them into our plane. Thousands of letters were waiting to be read, and none of the people they were addressed to would ever know what they had cost.
That same evening, back at Cap Juby, I sent a telegram to Toulouse.
It contained only a few words: 'Pilot killed. Plane broken. Mail intact. It is going on to Dakar.'

aient: have (sans qu'ils aient besoin = without their needing)
arrêtait: stopped (si le moteur s'arrêtait = if the engine stopped)
au: to the, at the, in the
avait-il: had he (peut-être avait-il trouvé = perhaps he had found)
basse: low (à voix basse = in a low voice)
cartes: cards (jouer aux cartes = to play cards)
celui: the one (celui que = the one that)
chez: at the home of (chez eux = at their place)
comme: like, as; how (comme c'est… ! = how … it is!)
continue: goes on (continue de vivre = lives on)
côté: side, way (de quel côté = which way)
dire: to say (il faut dire = it must be said)
distinguer: to tell apart, to make out
décider: to make up her mind (se décider à)
entier: whole (le monde entier = the whole world)
envie: desire (avoir envie de = to feel like)
espaces: spaces (les grands espaces = wide open spaces)
fallait: was necessary (il fallait que = had to)
fois: times (deux fois par semaine = twice a week)
gaz: throttle (réduire les gaz = to throttle back); gas
juby: Juby (cap Juby, on the Saharan coast)
levait: raised (lever les yeux = to look up)
lit: bed (aller au lit = to go to bed)
maison: home, house (à la maison = at home)
mal: trouble (avoir du mal à = to have trouble)
par: by, on (par terre = on the ground)
parlant: speaking (en lui parlant = speaking to him)
perte: loss (à perte de vue = as far as the eye can see)
plein: full (en plein soleil = in broad sunlight)
plus: more; no longer (ne … plus); most (le plus)
posés: se poser · past participle, m. pl.
punir: to punish (se faire punir = to get punished)
quittait: left (ne quittait pas d'une semelle = never left her side)
rend: makes (le rend calme = makes him calm)
reprendre: to get back (reprendre son souffle = to get your breath back)
restait: remained, was left (il en restait = there were … left)
route: way (en route pour = on the way to)
réduit: comes down to (se réduit à); reduces
sens: meaning (perdu son sens = lost its meaning)
serré: squeezed (serrer la main = to shake hands)
seules: only (seules les aiguilles = only the needles)
signe: sign (faire un signe de la main = to wave)
su: known (je ne l'ai jamais su = I never found out)
suffisait: was enough (il lui suffisait de = all she had to do was)
séparent: separate (les séparent de = stand between them and)
transporte: carries (on ne transporte pas = you can't carry)
trouve: find (pour qu'on ne le trouve pas = so that it wouldn't be found)
tue: kill (que je me tue = that I kill myself)
vole: steals (on se vole = you steal from yourself)
vouloir: to mean to (sans le vouloir = without meaning to)
voyait: could see (on y voyait = you could see)
vue: sight (à perte de vue = as far as the eye can see)
vus: seen (vus d'avion = seen from a plane)
